title: Piano Sonata in B minor
hook: Four movements folded into one, built from a handful of notes that keep changing shape.

painting.title: Christ Asleep during the Tempest
painting.collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
painting.pairingNote: Painted in the same year Liszt finished the sonata, a storm with one still figure at its centre; the sonata, too, rages and then ends in quiet.

facts: Liszt finished the sonata in Weimar, where he was court music director; the manuscript is dated 2 February 1853. He had spent the 1830s and 1840s as the most famous touring pianist in Europe.

He dedicated it to Robert Schumann, in return for Schumann’s *Fantasie* in C, which had been dedicated to him. When the printed copy reached Schumann’s house in May 1854, Schumann had already been taken to the asylum at Endenich.

It is one movement of about half an hour, but it holds a whole sonata inside it: a fast opening, a slow movement in the middle, a quick fugue that works like a [[scherzo|scherzo]], and a finale. Almost everything grows from three or four short [[motif|motif]]s that keep changing character.

Hans von Bülow gave the first public performance, in Berlin in January 1857. Critics were hostile: Eduard Hanslick wrote that anyone who heard it and found it beautiful was beyond help. The story goes that the young Brahms fell asleep when Liszt played it to him in 1853. Today it is one of the summits of the piano repertoire.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a dark question and a defiant answer (0:00), a hymn and a love song (≈ 3:00–5:00), a still, glowing slow section (≈ 12:15), a whispered fugue and a race to the top (≈ 19:35), and a quiet ending (last three minutes).

movements.heading: Lento assai – Allegro energico – Andante sostenuto – Allegro energico – Lento assai
movements.tempo: Lento assai – Allegro energico – Andante sostenuto – Allegro energico – Lento assai
movements.summary: One unbroken half hour for one player. The sonata opens with a soft, sinking scale and two angry ideas, and then spends its whole length transforming them: the same few notes become a hymn, a love song, a whispered fugue and, at the very end, a farewell. The big shape is [[sonata-form|sonata form]], with the slow movement and the scherzo set inside it. Because it is a single track, the times below are your map.

mainIdeas.name: The falling scale
mainIdeas.description: after two soft, detached notes in the bass, a slow scale sinks downward, quiet and uncertain. It returns at every turning point.

mainIdeas.name: The defiant leap
mainIdeas.description: loud octaves that jump up and fall in a jagged line, *Allegro energico*.

mainIdeas.name: The hammer blow
mainIdeas.description: one note repeated low in the bass, then a quick, mocking turn. Liszt called it *Hammerschlag*.

mainIdeas.name: The hymn
mainIdeas.description: a broad, solemn melody in full chords, marked *Grandioso*, in D major.

stops.hear: Two soft, short notes, low down; then a slow scale sinks into the bass, twice
stops.happening: The introduction, *Lento assai*. The falling scale

stops.hear: Suddenly loud: octaves leap and fall in a jagged, defiant phrase
stops.happening: The defiant leap. The main section begins, *Allegro energico*

stops.hear: Deep in the bass, a note hammered out several times, then a quick, sneering turn
stops.happening: The hammer blow, the third idea

stops.hear: The ideas chase each other; storms of octaves rise and break, then fall back
stops.happening: The first theme group, in B minor. The [[exposition|exposition]]

stops.hear: Everything broadens: a slow, ringing melody in loud, full chords, like a hymn with bells
stops.happening: The *Grandioso* hymn, in D major. The first firm ground in a major key

stops.hear: The hammer-blow idea comes back slow, soft and singing, like a love song
stops.happening: *Cantando espressivo*. The same notes, a new character: [[thematic-transformation|thematic transformation]]

stops.hear: Storms and lulls; the ideas are broken up, thrown together and pushed into new keys. At one point the music almost speaks, in free, broken phrases
stops.happening: The [[development|development]], with a short passage in the style of a [[recitative|recitative]]

stops.hear: Sudden stillness: a new, very quiet melody in the middle of the piano, warm and far away
stops.happening: *Andante sostenuto*, in F-sharp major. The slow movement inside the sonata

stops.hear: The love song returns, even softer and more private
The hymn breaks out at full power, the loudest moment so far; then it melts away
stops.happening: The climax of the slow section

stops.hear: The falling scale from the opening, slow and hushed
stops.happening: The introduction returns, as a hinge

stops.hear: Quick, dry, quiet notes: the defiant leap and the hammer blow enter one voice at a time, like a round
stops.happening: A [[fugato|fugato]] in B-flat minor. It is the scherzo, and the start of the [[recapitulation|recapitulation]]

stops.hear: The leap and the hammer blows crash back in B minor
The hymn again, now in B major
The love song again, in B major
Faster and faster: octaves race up and down the whole keyboard
One last, enormous statement of the hymn; then a sudden silence

stops.label: Last three minutes
stops.hear: The quiet melody of the slow section; the hammer blow, now soft, in the bass; the falling scale once more; soft high chords, and a single low B
stops.happening: The [[coda|coda]]. Liszt first wrote a loud ending, then crossed it out

notice: Follow the hammer blow. It begins as a sneer in the bass, becomes a love song at ≈ 4:30, and at the end is only a soft knock under quiet chords.
Listen to the very first and very last minutes. The sonata ends with the sounds it began with: the falling scale and soft, low notes.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Zimerman recorded the sonata in Copenhagen in February and March 1990. On the Spotify album it is a single track (track 1), followed by four of Liszt’s late pieces. On the CD the track carried index marks at the start of the slow section and of the fugue, which is why those two stops are the safest guides.

threads.title: A few notes, many faces
threads.body: Nearly every theme in the sonata is one of the opening ideas in disguise. Liszt’s name for this way of working was the transformation of themes.

threads.title: Four in one
threads.body: Fast, slow, scherzo, finale: the shape of a classical sonata, folded into a single span with no breaks.

threads.title: The silence after the storm
threads.body: The loudest climax, near the end, is followed not by triumph but by stillness.
